title: What is ASP.NET Core?
description: Get a clear, beginner-friendly introduction to ASP.NET Core — what it is, why it exists, and what you can build with it. Learn about its cross-platform design, high performance, and the modern developer experience it offers.

blocks.text: ASP.NET Core is a **modern, open-source, cross-platform framework** developed by Microsoft for building web applications, APIs, and cloud-based services. Unlike its predecessor ASP.NET, which ran only on Windows, ASP.NET Core runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux — giving developers true freedom in their tooling choices.

At its core, ASP.NET Core provides everything you need to build a web application: a server to handle HTTP requests, middleware to process those requests, and a rich ecosystem of libraries for common tasks like authentication, database access, and real-time communication.

The web development landscape has changed dramatically over the last decade. Developers need frameworks that are fast, flexible, and capable of running anywhere. ASP.NET Core was designed from the ground up to meet these demands.

blocks.title: Key reasons to choose ASP.NET Core
items: **High performance** — consistently ranks among the fastest web frameworks in independent benchmarks like TechEmpower
**Cross-platform** — develop and deploy on Windows, macOS, or Linux without changes to your code
**Open source** — fully open-source on GitHub with an active community contributing improvements
**Modern C# features** — leverages the latest C# language features including async/await, records, and pattern matching
**Unified MVC and Web API** — one framework for both browser-based pages and JSON APIs
**Built-in dependency injection** — encourages loose coupling and testable code from day one

blocks.text: ASP.NET Core is not limited to one type of application. Its flexibility makes it suitable for a wide range of projects, from simple websites to complex enterprise systems.

blocks.title: Common use cases
items: **Websites** — server-rendered pages using the MVC pattern with Razor views
**REST APIs** — JSON-based backends for mobile apps, SPAs, or other services
**Real-time apps** — SignalR for chat, live dashboards, and collaborative tools
**Microservices** — lightweight, independently deployable services in a larger architecture
**Blazor apps** — interactive client-side UIs using C# instead of JavaScript

blocks.title: A quick reality check
blocks.text: You do not need to master every part of ASP.NET Core before building something useful. Start with the basics — a simple MVC website or a basic API — and expand your knowledge as your project grows. The framework is designed to be progressive, so you can adopt more advanced features when you need them.

blocks.title: Minimal API — Hello World
blocks.content: The absolute simplest ASP.NET Core application using the minimal API style introduced in .NET 6.

blocks.text: This code creates a web server that listens for HTTP GET requests to the root URL (`/`) and responds with the text `Hello World!`. It uses the **minimal API** style, which is perfect for quick prototyping, microservices, and learning the basics.

blocks.title: Minimal API vs. MVC
blocks.text: The minimal API style above is great for small services, but for larger applications with many pages, you will want the full MVC pattern with Controllers, Views, and Models. Both styles are first-class citizens in ASP.NET Core and can even coexist in the same project.
Throughout this course, you will encounter several foundational concepts. Here is a preview of the most important ones so you know what to expect:

terms.definition: Software components that are assembled into an application pipeline to handle requests and responses. Each middleware component decides whether to pass the request to the next component.
A design pattern where objects receive their dependencies from an external source rather than creating them internally. ASP.NET Core has built-in DI support.
The mechanism that maps incoming HTTP request URLs to specific controller actions, determining which code handles each request.
A markup syntax for embedding C# code into HTML files. Razor views are the default way to generate dynamic HTML in ASP.NET Core MVC.
The process of converting HTTP request data (form fields, query strings, route data) into .NET objects that your action methods can work with.

blocks.text: This course follows a hands-on, progressive approach. Each module builds on the previous one, so we recommend completing them in order. You will write real code, build a working application step by step, and reinforce your learning with exercises at the end of each lesson.

blocks.title: Course structure at a glance
items: **Module 1: Getting Started** — set up your tools and build your first project
**Module 2: MVC Fundamentals** — understand the Model-View-Controller pattern
**Module 3: Routing and URLs** — control how users navigate your app
**Module 4: Model Binding and Validation** — process and validate user data
**Module 5: Razor Views** — create dynamic HTML pages
**Module 6: Dependency Injection** — write testable, maintainable code

items.text: I can explain what ASP.NET Core is and what it is used for
items.hint: Focus on cross-platform, high-performance, open-source web framework for apps and APIs

items.hint: MVC uses controllers, views, and models; minimal API uses a single Program.cs file

items.text: I can name at least three types of applications built with ASP.NET Core
items.hint: Websites, REST APIs, real-time apps, microservices, and Blazor apps

items.text: I have written and run a minimal 'Hello World' ASP.NET Core app
items.hint: Use var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args) and app.MapGet("/", ...)

blocks.title: Write Your First ASP.NET Core App
blocks.description: If you already have the .NET SDK installed, try running a minimal API locally to see ASP.NET Core in action.
steps: Open a terminal and run `dotnet --version` to confirm the SDK is installed (version 7.0 or later recommended)
Create a new folder called `hello-aspnet` and navigate into it
Create a new file called `Program.cs` and paste the minimal API example shown above
Run the app with the command `dotnet run`
Open a browser and navigate to `https://localhost:5000` (or the URL shown in the terminal)
Confirm you see the text "Hello World!" displayed in your browser
blocks.expectedOutcome: You should see "Hello World!" in your browser, confirming that ASP.NET Core is running and responding to HTTP requests. The terminal output should show the listening URLs.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary
points: ASP.NET Core is a modern, cross-platform, open-source framework for building web apps and APIs
It offers high performance, built-in dependency injection, and first-class support for both MVC and minimal API styles
You can build websites, REST APIs, real-time apps, microservices, and Blazor apps
A complete web server can be written in as few as five lines of C# code using minimal APIs
The course covers progressively more advanced topics: setup, MVC, routing, Razor views, and dependency injection
blocks.takeaway: ASP.NET Core is a versatile, high-performance framework that removes the traditional Windows-only limitation of ASP.NET, opening modern web development to developers on any platform.
